# KOJOH: every project in detail

Source: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects. All datasets are synthetic. Prices in Indian rupees.

## Late Again: Last-Mile Delivery in Tier-2 India
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/late-again-last-mile-fy2526
Track: Business / Ops | Level: hard | Price: Rs 249 | Tools: Python, SQL, Excel | Good for: Data Analyst, Operations Analyst
Dataset: 14,750 rows, 41 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A logistics analytics project on a year of dispatch data from a regional courier in tier-2 India: 14,750 rows and 41 columns. The on-time number on the dashboard is wrong, and the biggest client is unhappy. You compute on-time delivery properly, find what sits behind the best-looking riders and show which shipments lose money.

What is messy in the data:
- About 190 shipments entered twice with the same AWB number
- Six date columns in five formats; a few deliveries dated before pickup
- The month label blank on about 40% of rows
- Each shipper under about 5 spellings; pincodes as 273001, 273001.0, 273 001
- Weights as 0.5, 0.50 kg, 500 g, 500gm, and some zero weights

Project ideas it covers: Last-mile delivery performance; Measuring on-time delivery correctly; Rider and hub performance; COD vs prepaid failures and RTO; Profitability by weight, zone and service.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How should on-time delivery be measured, and how can it be gamed? How would you find a rider whose good numbers hide a problem? Which shipments lose money and how did you find them?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Data | Phase 2, SQL: Answer the Business Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Shipment Lookup | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Analytics | Phase 4, Documentation

## Slow Boat from Ningbo: China Import Procurement Tracker
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/slow-boat-from-ningbo-fy2526
Track: Business / Ops | Level: hard | Price: Rs 449 | Tools: Python, SQL, Excel, Power BI | Good for: Business Analyst, Supply Chain Analyst, Operations Analyst, Data Analyst
Dataset: 24,392 rows, 36 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A supply chain project on 470 China import purchase orders across six messy files: 24,392 rows. The head of supply chain needs to know where every container is, which documents and payments are overdue and how much cash is needed. You rebuild the picture as of your own report date and deliver a tracker, chase lists and a cash plan.

What is messy in the data:
- Purchase orders revised as 260411, 260411.R, 260411.R.1; only the latest counts
- Up to seven spellings per supplier factory; ports written four ways
- Money in USD and INR text in six formats; five date formats including Excel serials
- Contact name, email and phone crammed into one cell in four layouts
- Product code blank on about 6% and line value blank on about 7% of rows

Project ideas it covers: Import shipment tracking; Supplier delay analysis; Documents and payments chase list; Cash flow planning for imports; As-of-date reporting.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How do you build a report as it looked on a past date? How would you rank suppliers on delivery reliability? What would you put on a procurement control tower?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean and Join the Data | Phase 2, SQL: Answer the Business Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: PO and Container Lookup | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Control Tower | Phase 4, Documentation

## Kirana Store Sales: A Lucknow General Store's Year of Bills
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/kirana-store-sales-free
Track: Data Analyst | Level: beginner | Price: free | Tools: Python, SQL, Excel, Power BI | Good for: Data Analyst, Business Analyst
Dataset: 9,629 rows, 11 columns | Tasks: 18 | Time: about 6 to 10 hours

In short: A free beginner project on a year of bills from a Lucknow kirana store: 9,629 rows across three files. The owner wants to know which items really make money, when the shop is busiest and how much is stuck in customer credit (udhaar). You clean the bills in Python, answer the questions in SQL and build a two page dashboard.

What is messy in the data:
- Item names typed by hand in several spellings each (case, spacing and short forms), matched to an item master
- Loose items sold in mixed units: 0.5 kg, 500 gm, 2 pcs
- Prices as text: 54, ₹54, Rs.54, 54.00
- Three date formats and two time formats (24-hour and AM/PM)
- About 2% of rows are exact duplicates (double-printed bills); returns carry negative quantities
- Amount blank on about 5% of rows; customer names like Gupta ji and first names only

Project ideas it covers: Retail sales analysis for a small shop; Profit vs revenue by product; Customer credit (udhaar) tracking; Busiest hours and staffing analysis; Festival (Diwali) sales impact.
Interview questions it prepares you for: Which products sell a lot but make little profit, and how did you find them? How did you deal with item names typed in many different ways? How would you decide when a shop needs a second cashier?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Billing Data | Phase 2, SQL: Answer Sharma ji's Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard: The Shop | Phase 3b, Dashboard: The Udhaar Book | Phase 4, Documentation

## The Quiet Quitters: Streaming App Churn Prediction, India
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/the-quiet-quitters-ott-churn
Track: Data Scientist | Level: hard | Price: Rs 249 | Tools: Python, SQL, Machine Learning, Power BI | Good for: Data Scientist, Data Analyst
Dataset: 223,838 rows, 26 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A data science project on four messy exports from an Indian streaming app: 223,838 rows. The business wants to know who will cancel and which saves are worth paying for. You build an honest churn label, leak-free features and a model tested on a later time window, then turn the scores into a call list worth rupees.

What is messy in the data:
- Customer IDs as CP100123, cp100123, CP-100123 and with leading spaces
- Five date formats including Excel serials; ages like 24 yrs, 999 or blank
- Plans under about 12 spellings and billing cycles under about 11
- Watch time as 12.5, 12.5 hrs or 750 min
- Ticket categories under about 22 spellings; satisfaction score only 35% filled
- Columns that describe what happened after the prediction date (leakage)

Project ideas it covers: Customer churn prediction; Leak-free feature engineering; Voluntary vs involuntary churn; Time-based model validation; Turning model scores into a business call list.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How do you make sure a churn model has no data leakage? Why use a time-based split instead of a random split? How would you turn churn scores into a decision with a rupee value?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean, Label and Build Features | Phase 2, SQL and Modelling: Understand and Predict the Churn | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Subscriber and Call List | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Model and Money | Phase 4, Documentation

## The Diwali Discount Trap: E-commerce Appliance Orders, India
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/diwali-discount-trap-fy2526
Track: Data Analyst | Level: hard | Price: Rs 249 | Tools: Python, SQL, Excel, Power BI | Good for: Data Analyst
Dataset: 14,891 rows, 41 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: An e-commerce analytics project on a year of marketplace orders from an Indian appliance brand: 14,891 rows and 41 columns. The biggest sales month lost money and nobody can say why. You clean the orders, compute contribution margin and find the discount level where extra sales stop paying.

What is messy in the data:
- About 190 orders pasted in twice with the same Order ID
- Ten money columns in several text formats and five date formats including Excel serials
- The month label blank on about 40% of rows
- Each of 20 listing managers under about 8 name spellings; employee code blank on about 5%
- Marketplaces and categories under about 5 spellings each; discount as 40%, 0.4000, 40.0 %
- Order status under about 25 spellings

Project ideas it covers: E-commerce discount and profitability analysis; Contribution margin by month and category; Returns, RTO and COD leakage; Marketing channel ROAS; Listing manager performance ranking.
Interview questions it prepares you for: Why can the biggest revenue month lose money? How would you find the discount level where extra sales stop paying? How do you rank sales staff fairly: by revenue or by contribution?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Data | Phase 2, SQL: Answer the Business Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Order Lookup | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Analytics | Phase 4, Documentation

## The ₹176 Lakh Question: Tata Dealership Sales, Delhi
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/tata-delhi-sales-fy2526
Track: Data Analyst | Level: hard | Price: Rs 449 | Tools: Python, SQL | Good for: Data Analyst
Dataset: 14,735 rows, 41 columns | Tasks: 41 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A sales analytics project on a year of hand-typed ERP entries from an 8-branch car dealer group in Delhi: 14,735 rows and 41 columns. Management cannot agree who really performed or what the record month cost. You clean the entries, rank salespeople fairly and write the recommendation that settles the bonus argument.

What is messy in the data:
- About 190 deals entered twice with the same Deal ID
- Booking dates in five formats including Excel serials and month names only
- Each of 56 salespeople under about 8 name spellings
- Employee codes blank on about 5%, some lower case, some mistyped (EMP01023)
- Money stored as text in several formats

Project ideas it covers: Sales performance and incentive analysis; Discounts and margin by month; Salesperson identity cleaning; Branch and model performance; Old stock vs new stock buyers.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How do you clean salesperson names typed eight different ways? Why can a record sales month be a bad month? How would you rank salespeople for a bonus?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Data | Phase 2, SQL: Answer the Business Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Deal Lookup | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Analytics | Phase 4, Documentation

## Stockout Saturdays: Quick Commerce Demand Forecasting, India
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/stockout-saturdays-quick-commerce
Track: Data Scientist | Level: hard | Price: Rs 249 | Tools: Python, SQL, Machine Learning, Power BI | Good for: Data Scientist, Supply Chain Analyst, Data Analyst
Dataset: 93,370 rows, 10 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A data science project on 93,370 store-SKU days from a quick commerce (10-minute grocery) app. Sales are capped on days the shelves run empty, so the busiest days can look slow. You estimate the real demand, build a forecast that beats a simple baseline and show what it changes for the stores.

What is messy in the data:
- Units sold capped on stockout days, so sales are not demand
- Three date formats; store codes as BLR-KOR and BLR_KOR
- Units as 12 or 12.0; promo flags as Y, Yes, N or blank
- Closing stock blank on about 7% and hours in stock blank on about 10% of rows

Project ideas it covers: Demand forecasting with stockouts; Censored demand estimation; Festival, promo and event effects; Forecast accuracy (WAPE) vs a baseline; Inventory planning recommendations.
Interview questions it prepares you for: Why is sales data not the same as demand, and how did you adjust for it? How do you evaluate a forecast fairly? What features would you use for daily store-level demand?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean, Uncensor and Build Features | Phase 2, SQL and Modelling: Understand and Forecast | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Store and SKU Explorer | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Supply Control Room | Phase 4, Documentation

## Approved Only: NBFC Personal Loan Credit Scoring, India
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/approved-only-nbfc-credit-risk
Track: Data Scientist | Level: hard | Price: Rs 449 | Tools: Python, SQL, Machine Learning, Statistics | Good for: Data Scientist, Data Analyst
Dataset: 180,467 rows, 18 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A data science project on 180,467 rows from an Indian NBFC's personal loan book. Only approved loans have outcomes, recent loans have not had time to go bad and some columns leak the answer. You build a credit scoring model the honest way, calibrate it and choose an approval cut-off with real profit numbers.

What is messy in the data:
- Income in monthly and annual forms: 45k, 5.4 L p.a., Rs 45,000/month, 5,40,000 annual
- Bureau score NH, -1, 000 or blank all mean no credit history
- Employment type under about 20 spellings
- Resubmitted applications (IDs ending in R) and five date formats
- Columns known only after the decision, which leak the answer
- Outcomes only for approved loans (selection bias)

Project ideas it covers: Credit scoring and default prediction; Selection bias and reject inference; Vintage analysis; Model calibration; Approval cut-off with profit economics.
Interview questions it prepares you for: What is selection bias in credit data and how does it affect your model? How do you choose an approval cut-off? How do you check whether model scores are calibrated?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean, Label and Build Features | Phase 2, SQL and Modelling: Understand and Score the Risk | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Application Scorer | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Portfolio and Model | Phase 4, Documentation

## The Funnel That Leaked: App Onboarding and an A/B Test
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/the-funnel-that-leaked-free
Track: Product Analyst | Level: beginner | Price: free | Tools: Python, SQL, Statistics | Good for: Product Analyst, Data Analyst
Dataset: 41,268 rows, 11 columns | Tasks: 19 | Time: about 6 to 10 hours

In short: A free product analytics project on 41,268 raw app events from a savings app's six-step onboarding funnel and an A/B test. The dashboard says the new screen lost, and you find out what really happened. You clean the events in Python, rebuild the funnel and the test in SQL, and write an experiment readout.

What is messy in the data:
- Six funnel steps written under about 12 event-name spellings
- Two timestamp styles: Android in UTC with Z, iOS in India time with no zone
- About 1,556 retried duplicate events sent seconds after the original
- Internal test accounts (test_qa...) mixed in with real users
- Variants written as A/B and as control/treatment

Project ideas it covers: Onboarding funnel analysis; A/B test analysis with real pitfalls; Event data cleaning; Conversion by platform and source; Experiment readout for a product manager.
Interview questions it prepares you for: What would you check before trusting an A/B test result? How do you build a funnel from raw event logs? Explain Simpson's paradox with an example you found.

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Event Stream | Phase 2, SQL: Read the Funnel and the Test | Phase 3a, Dashboard: The Funnel | Phase 3b, Dashboard: The Experiment | Phase 4, Documentation

## Spares Never Arrive: Appliance Service and Spare Parts TAT, India
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/spares-never-arrive-fy2526
Track: Business / Ops | Level: hard | Price: Rs 249 | Tools: Python, SQL, Excel, Power BI | Good for: Operations Analyst, Business Analyst, Data Analyst
Dataset: 26,746 rows, 17 columns | Tasks: 40 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: An operations analytics project on about 17,000 appliance service tickets and the spare part orders behind them: 26,746 rows. Reported repair times look fine, but customers say otherwise. You rebuild the true turnaround time and find whether delays come from the warehouse, the courier or the service centre.

What is messy in the data:
- About 1.5% of service tickets are duplicates
- Five date formats including Excel serials
- Customer names in about eight spellings each; products like MIXER GRINDER, MixerGrinder, Mixer
- Ticket status under about 12 spellings; some centres close tickets before the repair
- Repeat complaints only mentioned in free-text remarks; ticket IDs as SR-2500001 and SR2500001

Project ideas it covers: Service turnaround time (TAT) analysis; Spare parts delay root cause; Service centre performance ranking; Repeat complaint detection; Customer rating vs delay.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How would you measure turnaround time honestly when tickets are closed early? How do you rank service centres fairly? How did you find repeat complaints in free text?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean and Link the Cases | Phase 2, SQL: Find Where the Days Go | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Case Lookup | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Service Control Room | Phase 4, Documentation

## Where Did My Salary Go: UPI and Bank Statements of 24 First-Jobbers
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/where-did-my-salary-go-fy2526
Track: Data Analyst | Level: beginner | Price: Rs 99 | Tools: Python, SQL, Excel, Power BI | Good for: Data Analyst, Business Analyst
Dataset: 16,448 rows, 15 columns | Tasks: 42 | Time: about 6 to 10 hours

In short: A beginner data analyst project on 12 months of bank and UPI statements from 24 first-jobbers across five banks: 16,448 rows. The question is where each person's salary goes, which subscriptions they forgot and which charges hit twice. You parse five bank formats, build trustworthy categories and show each person their money.

What is messy in the data:
- Five banks, five date formats and five narration layouts in one export
- Debit and credit in separate columns for some banks, one signed amount with (Dr)/(Cr) for others
- 544 duplicate rows from overlapping monthly downloads
- The app's own category blank on about 22% of rows and wrong on about 1 in 10
- Merchants hidden inside narrations and UPI IDs (swiggy@ybl)

Project ideas it covers: Personal finance and spending analysis; Parsing bank statement narrations; Subscription and recurring payment detection; Double charge detection; Savings rate dashboard.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How did you turn messy bank narrations into merchants and categories? How do you tell an export duplicate from a real double charge? What would you show a user to help them save more?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Statements | Phase 2, SQL: Answer the Money Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard Page 1: Person View | Phase 3b, Dashboard Page 2: Cohort View | Phase 4, Documentation

## Aai's Tiffin Service: A Pune Home Kitchen's Order Sheet
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/aai-tiffin-service-free
Track: Business / Ops | Level: beginner | Price: free | Tools: Excel, Power BI | Good for: Business Analyst, Data Analyst, Operations Analyst
Dataset: 25,775 rows, 24 columns | Tasks: 18 | Time: about 6 to 10 hours

In short: A free Excel and Power BI project on a year of orders from a Pune home tiffin service: 25,775 rows typed into one sheet by three people. The owner wants to know which plans and areas make money, whether a price rise drove customers away and who owes her. You clean the sheet with lookups, answer the questions with PivotTables and SUMIFS, and build a two page Power BI dashboard.

What is messy in the data:
- Four date styles plus Excel serial numbers like 45762
- Plans written as Veg Basic, Basic, VB; areas like Hinjewadi, Hinjawadi, Hinjewadi Ph 1
- About 2.5% of rows are double entries typed again with a new ID
- Prices as 90, ₹90, Rs 90, 90/-, blank on about 3% of rows
- Phones as 9876543210, +91 9876543210, 98765 43210 or blank
- Old prices still typed for weeks after a price rise

Project ideas it covers: Small business sales analysis in Excel; Customer dues and collections tracker; Price increase impact analysis; Area and plan profitability; Power BI dashboard for a small business.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How did you clean dates typed in four different styles in Excel? How would you measure whether a price increase lost customers? Walk me through a SUMIFS you built and why.

Phases: Phase 1, Excel: Clean the Order Sheet | Phase 2, Excel: Formulas and PivotTables | Phase 3a, Power BI: The Business | Phase 3b, Power BI: The Dues Tracker | Phase 4, Documentation

## The Migration That Lost Students: Reconcile Two Systems with SQL
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/migration-lost-students-free
Track: Data Engineer | Level: beginner | Price: free | Tools: SQL, Data Quality, Data Engineering | Good for: Data Engineer, Quality Analyst, Data Analyst
Dataset: 9,648 rows, 34 columns | Tasks: 18 | Time: about 6 to 10 hours

In short: A free SQL and data quality project on 9,648 rows from a Jaipur coaching institute that moved its students and fee receipts to a new app. Students went missing, some were created twice and the rupee totals stopped matching. You reconcile both systems in SQL, put a number on every problem and write the data quality checks that would have caught them.

What is messy in the data:
- The same student keyed as DJ/2025/0123 in one system and DJ-2025-123 in the other
- The legacy roll number blank on about 6% of new-app records
- Some students missing from the new app and some created twice
- Money in rupees on one side and paise on the other, with one batch saved 100 times too small
- Names in capitals on one side, title case (sometimes surname first) on the other

Project ideas it covers: Data migration reconciliation; Writing data quality checks in SQL; Finding duplicates and missing records; Unit and format bugs in money data; Incident write-up for a data issue.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How would you reconcile two systems that should hold the same data? Name five data quality checks you would run every night and why. How do you match records when the key was reformatted?

Phases: Phase 1, SQL: Load, Profile and Match | Phase 2, SQL: Reconcile and Test | Phase 3a, Dashboard: Reconciliation | Phase 3b, Dashboard: Data Quality Board | Phase 4, Documentation

## Returns Are Eating Our Profit: An Online Fashion Store in the US, UK and EU
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/returns-eating-profit-free
Track: Data Analyst | Level: beginner | Price: free | Tools: Excel, SQL, Power BI | Good for: Data Analyst, Business Analyst, E-commerce Analyst
Dataset: 20,441 rows, 32 columns | Tasks: 18 | Time: about 6 to 10 hours

In short: A free beginner project on a year of orders and returns from a fictional online fashion store selling in the US, UK and EU. The founder thinks returns are eating the profit, and you find out where. You fix three date formats and three currencies, then show returns by product, size, reason and discount code in Excel or SQL and Power BI.

What is messy in the data:
- Dates month-first in the US file, day-first in the UK file and ISO or dd.mm.yyyy in the EU file
- Prices as $48.99, £38.99, 45,99 € and 48.99 USD
- 236 order lines exported twice
- Countries as USA, U.S., GB, Deutschland, Holland; sizes as Small, SM, W30, EU 38
- Returns with # order numbers, blank SKUs and 30 that match no order
- Return reasons in free text: Runs small, changed my mind, Faulty

Project ideas it covers: E-commerce sales and returns analysis; Return rate by product, size and reason; Multi-currency data cleaning; Profit after returns; Discount code impact analysis.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How would you handle dates written month-first in one file and day-first in another? How do you calculate a return rate, and what goes in the denominator? How would you measure whether discounts attract customers who return more?

Phases: Phase 1, Clean the Orders and Returns | Phase 2, Answer the Business Questions | Phase 3a, Dashboard: Sales | Phase 3b, Dashboard: Returns | Phase 4, Documentation

## The Price Rise That Cost Us: SaaS Subscriptions, MRR and Churn
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/price-rise-saas-mrr
Track: Product Analyst | Level: intermediate | Price: Rs 349 | Tools: Python, SQL, Power BI | Good for: Product Analyst, Data Analyst, Business Analyst
Dataset: 51,731 rows, 31 columns | Tasks: 20 | Time: about 10 to 15 hours

In short: A product analytics project on two years of billing events, invoices and usage from a fictional B2B SaaS app with customers in over a dozen countries. The CEO says a price rise worked and customer success says it did not. You build MRR, the MRR bridge, churn and cohort retention, then settle the argument with numbers.

What is messy in the data:
- 137 billing events sent twice by webhook retries, and the file is not in time order
- Event times in ISO, +00:00 style and Unix seconds
- Amounts in cents on some rows and dollars on others; yearly plans stored as the yearly amount
- Event types written three ways each (customer.subscription.deleted, canceled, cancelled)
- 28 internal test accounts mixed in with customers
- Account ids as ACC-00123, acc-00123, ACC00123

Project ideas it covers: SaaS MRR and ARR reporting; MRR bridge (new, expansion, contraction, churn); Cohort retention and NRR; Pricing change impact analysis; Involuntary churn and dunning analysis.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How do you calculate MRR from subscription events? What is the difference between NRR and GRR? How would you tell whether a price rise caused churn?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Clean the Billing Events | Phase 2, SQL: SaaS Metrics | Phase 3a, Dashboard: Account Lookup | Phase 3b, Dashboard: SaaS Metrics | Phase 4, Documentation

## Empty Chairs: Predicting Clinic Appointment No-Shows
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/empty-chairs-clinic-no-shows
Track: Data Scientist | Level: hard | Price: Rs 449 | Tools: Python, Machine Learning, Statistics | Good for: Data Scientist, Data Analyst
Dataset: 151,971 rows, 31 columns | Tasks: 20 | Time: about 15 to 25 hours

In short: A data science project on two years of appointments from six fictional outpatient clinics, where about one booked slot in six ends with an empty chair. You define an honest scoring moment and label, remove four planted leaks and validate on months the model has never seen. Then you turn calibrated scores into an overbooking rule worth money.

What is messy in the data:
- Four leaky columns: check-in time, visit minutes, co-pay collected and a total no-shows count that includes the future
- Three time formats, including month-first with AM/PM
- No-shows written as No Show, DNA, noshow
- Birth years of 1900 and 0, distances of -1 and 9999
- About 7% of reminders sent after the scoring moment
- Specialty and clinic names that change between systems

Project ideas it covers: Appointment no-show prediction; Finding and removing data leakage; Time-based model validation; Probability calibration; Overbooking decision rule with costs.
Interview questions it prepares you for: What is data leakage, and how did you find it in this project? Why use a time-based split instead of a random split? How do you turn model probabilities into a business decision?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: Population, Label and Leaks | Phase 2, Modelling: Honest Validation and Value | Phase 3a, Dashboard: The Call List | Phase 3b, Dashboard: The Model | Phase 4, Documentation

## Cold Fries: Food Delivery Times in Chicago, London and Singapore
URL: https://www.kojohhi.com/projects/cold-fries-food-delivery
Track: Business / Ops | Level: intermediate | Price: Rs 349 | Tools: Python, SQL, Power BI | Good for: Operations Analyst, Data Analyst, Business Analyst
Dataset: 177,728 rows, 31 columns | Tasks: 20 | Time: about 10 to 15 hours

In short: An operations project on four months of food delivery orders in Chicago, London and Singapore, logged on three different clocks. About one order in five arrives late, and each city blames something different. You put every timestamp on one clock, build a six-stage timeline for each order and find where the late minutes really go.

What is messy in the data:
- Three clocks: UTC, local time with no zone, and Unix epoch milliseconds
- Daylight saving ends on 26 October in London and 2 November in Chicago
- Chicago distances in miles, the rest in km; money in $, £ and S$
- About 1,800 blank Ready times and 3,400 pressed after the courier left
- 594 duplicate orders and 870 duplicate courier events
- City codes CHI, LDN, SG and three local date styles

Project ideas it covers: Delivery time and lateness analysis; Time zone and daylight saving data cleaning; Order timeline (stage) analysis; Batching and courier efficiency; Refund cost of late orders.
Interview questions it prepares you for: How do you combine timestamps logged in UTC, local time and epoch milliseconds? How would you find which stage of a process causes delays? How would you test whether batching orders hurts customers?

Phases: Phase 1, Python: One Clock for Everything | Phase 2, SQL: Where the Minutes Go | Phase 3a, Dashboard: Order Timeline | Phase 3b, Dashboard: Operations | Phase 4, Documentation
